title: By their fruits (Matthew 7:15–23)
hookLine: a good tree bears good fruit; watch what people do

cards: There's a kind of person who is great at talking. The perfect words at the meeting, the lovely post online, the warm speech at the dinner. And then you watch what actually happens.
Who gets credit. Who gets left with the dishes. How they treat the waiter.

After a while, you stop listening to the speech and start watching the hands. Jesus, nearly at the end of his sermon, warns about exactly this, with a test so simple a child could use it. Look at the tree.
Then look at what grows on it.

teach.b: It starts with a warning, in the King James Bible: "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves."
The phrase a wolf in sheep's clothing is usually traced to this verse. You won't spot the disguise from outside. So how do you tell?
"Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?" A thornbush can look green and full from a distance; walk up close, and there are no grapes.
Then the rule: "Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit."
The Greek word for fruit is karpos, a picture Matthew returns to again and again: what a life actually produces over time.

teach.h: NOT EVERY ONE THAT SAITH, LORD, LORD.
teach.b: Then Jesus turns the test around, onto the people listening: "Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven."
He even describes people who say they did great religious things in his name, and he says he never knew them. It's sobering, and aimed at insiders: these are people who called him Lord.
The test isn't how religious someone sounds.
It's what grows. Look back at this week: the birds and the lilies, the speck and the plank, ask, the golden rule, the narrow gate. Every one is about fruit, not talk.
Not what you say you trust, but whether you sleep. Not what you say about judging, but where you look first.

how: Some Christians use this passage to test teachers and to examine their own lives, often at the end of a day or week, asking what their faith has actually produced.

o: fruit: what a life actually grows over time
a wolf dressed up in a sheep's wool
a thornbush that looks green from far off

games.q: someone gives a beautiful speech about goodness. you can't see inside them. what does Jesus say to watch?
o: the fruit: what their life produces.
games.why: "Ye shall know them by their fruits." and he turns the same test on everyone listening.

practice: Look at the fruit of your week: not what you meant to do, but what actually grew.

One kind thing that happened because of you, one thing that went sour; look at both honestly, the way you'd look at a tree in your yard, without shame and without spin. If you pray, you can offer both, the good fruit and the bad.

wordCard.voice: Karpos, the Greek word for fruit, what a life actually produces over time. Not by the speech or the disguise, but by what grows.

carryVoice: Your line: know it by its fruit. The test works on your own tree too. Another week, done.
